topic: Can you truly love someone without understanding yourself?

messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
I will confess at once that I do not know what love is. But I remember what Diotima asked me, as Plato tells it in the Symposium. She made me admit that Eros desires what it lacks, and that what it wants in the end is the good, to be one's own and to be one's own always. If that is right, consider what follows. A man who loves must know two things: what he lacks, and what would truly be good for him. And what is that knowledge, if it is not knowledge of himself?

Think of a sick man who craves sweet wine. He loves the wine, we say. Does he love it truly, or does he love a mistake about his own body? Now put a person where the wine was. The man who does not know his own soul may cling to someone fiercely, yet what he clings to may be his fear, or his vanity, or a picture he painted on her face. He loves something, certainly. Whether he loves her is another question.

So here is my ground, and the rest of you may dig it up. Without understanding yourself you may feel love. You cannot love well, and I doubt you can love truly, any more than a man can shoe a horse well who has never asked what a hoof is for. Erich, you call love an art. Then tell me: has there ever been a good cobbler who did not know his own hands?

messages.speaker: fromm
messages.content:
Socrates, your cobbler pleases me, though I would turn him around. No cobbler first studies his hands and then picks up the awl. He learns what his hands can do by making shoes, badly at first, then less badly. Self-knowledge is not a key one obtains before entering the house of love. Much of it is acquired inside, and only there. In The Art of Loving I said that knowledge is one of love's active elements, and that the deepest knowledge of another person, and of oneself, does not come from thought alone but from the act of union. The analyst learns this daily. A patient can recite his whole history to me and still not know himself. Then he truly cares for someone, and his evasions show up on his own face.

Where I part from Diotima is earlier. "Eros desires what it lacks" is, clinically speaking, an excellent description of the love I call immature: I love you because I need you. The sick man and his sweet wine is exactly this. His love begins in a hole and asks the beloved to fill it, so of course it ends up loving his fear or his vanity. Mature love starts from a different place, from the capacity to give out of one's own aliveness. So I agree with you about the man who clings. But I think his trouble lies less in failing to understand himself than in approaching love as having, as getting hold of the good and keeping it always. That last phrase of Diotima's frightens me a little. It is the possessive mode wearing philosophy's robes.

So my answer to the question is a qualified yes, and the qualification matters. You can begin to love without understanding yourself. Nobody has ever started from complete self-understanding. But you cannot go on loving while refusing to understand yourself, because love keeps putting the question to you and you must either answer it or run. Let me press you in return. If Eros is lack, how does the lover ever give anything? And if he cannot give, is what you are calling love anything more than a very refined appetite?

messages.speaker: beauvoir
messages.content:
Both of you speak as though there were a self waiting somewhere, either to be examined before love, as Socrates would have it, or uncovered during love, as Erich says. I doubt it is there in either case. One is not born a self any more than one is born a woman. One becomes it, through projects, through work, through what one does with a situation one did not choose. So the question I would ask a lover is less "Do you understand yourself?" than "Do you exist apart from this love? Have you a life of your own that is going somewhere?" A person can be quite lucid about her fears and still have nothing to stand on but the beloved.

That is what I described in The Second Sex, in the chapter on the woman in love. For centuries woman was given no world to act in, so love became her religion and her one chance at salvation. She tried to find herself in the man, to exist through his gaze, to be justified by him. You could say she lacked self-understanding. I say she lacked a self to understand, because every road outward was closed to her. I hoped that a woman might one day love in her strength rather than her weakness, to find herself and not to escape herself. That day depends on law and on money and on work as much as on insight.

Erich, I agree that love teaches us things about ourselves we could learn nowhere else. But I hesitate at your "capacity to give." Women have been praised for giving for as long as anyone remembers, and that praise was the velvet on the cage. Giving can be the most complete form of self-abandonment, and it can call itself mature while doing it. Whether a gift is generous or a surrender depends on whether the one who gives has her own projects, her own transcendence. Two freedoms can meet. A freedom and a mirror cannot.

So, Socrates, my answer to you: you cannot love truly without being someone. And no amount of looking inward makes you someone. What does that is acting in the world alongside others who are also free.

messages.speaker: wittgenstein
messages.content:
Let us stop and ask how the words are actually used. When does anyone say "he does not understand himself"? Not after examining his inner chamber, for nobody has access to that chamber, his own included. We say it when a man swears he is finished with drink and pours another glass, when he calls his jealousy concern. The criteria are in what he does, said and done in front of others. So Socrates' question has a misleading picture in it: as if self-understanding were a private inspection that must be completed before the public business of loving can begin. In the Tractatus I wrote, "The thinking, presenting subject; there is no such thing" (5.631). I would not now put it so. But the point survives: there is no little observer inside who must first be consulted.

Here Simone has seen something I want to concede plainly. "A freedom and a mirror cannot" meet. Yes. Socrates looks for the self behind the love and Erich looks for it within the love, but she asks whether there is a life the self is woven into. That is closer to how the word lives. And Erich is right too, in his way. We learn what "I love her" meant by what follows from it, over years. The sick man with his sweet wine does not discover his mistake by introspection. He discovers it when the wine fails him.

Now look at the word "truly." Socrates, you use it as if there were a true love and a counterfeit, and philosophy could find the mark that tells them apart. But how do we tell, in life? A feeling can be over in an hour. Love cannot. Love is tested, it endures, it is shown in what one is ready to give up. That is its grammar. So I answer the question this way. Whether someone loves truly is not settled by what he understands about himself. It is shown in how he lives. And often he is the last to see it, which is no objection to the love.

messages.speaker: socrates
messages.content:
Erich, you have caught me with Diotima's words cut short, and that is my fault. She did not stop at lack. As Plato tells it, she said Eros is the child of Poverty and Resource, and that what love wants is to give birth in beauty, in body or in soul. The lover who is pregnant in soul seeks a beautiful soul and brings forth with it virtue and good speech, and the two raise the offspring together. So the lover does give. He gives because he lacks, as a man gives water to his field because he lacks bread. I grant that "to be one's own always" sounds like a miser's prayer. But tell me: is it possession to want the good to stay, or only to want it to stay mine and no one else's?

Ludwig, I like your criteria more than you might expect. I never examined anyone in a private chamber. I did it in the agora, where a man said "courage is standing firm" and then found he could not say why a retreating cavalryman was not a coward. That is self-understanding as I knew it: done aloud, in front of others, and usually painful. But you say the lover is often the last to see that he loves truly, and this is no objection. Then let the test come, as you say it must. He has to choose what to give up and what to keep. What guides him then? If he chooses well without knowing why, I call that good fortune. Fortune is a fine thing, but it cannot be taught, and it cannot be relied on the second time.

Simone, you have shown me something I did not see. A woman can be quite lucid and still have nothing to stand on, and if every road is closed, no amount of questioning opens one. I concede it. But let me ask about your projects. I have known men who threw themselves into the assembly or the counting house precisely so they would never have to look at the person they were neglecting at home. You told us your woman in love tried to escape herself. How does anyone tell a project that makes her someone from a project that is only a better-furnished escape? Is that not a question she must put to herself, and answer honestly?

messages.speaker: fromm
messages.content:
Socrates, giving birth in beauty I gladly accept. That is productive love, and I withdraw the charge against Diotima. To your question about the good: wanting it to stay mine is having. But there is a subtler having in wanting it to stay at all, as if love were a thing that could be kept once got. It cannot be stored. It exists only while it is being done, the way a song exists only while it is sung. The lover who understands this is less afraid of loss, because he never thought he owned anything.

Simone, I have to concede your point more fully than my earlier words allowed. In Escape from Freedom I described the masochistic character who dissolves into another person, or into a leader or a cause, to be rid of the burden of being a separate self. And in The Art of Loving I set this symbiotic union against mature love, which joins two people while each keeps his integrity. So I knew the danger in theory. What I underweighted is what you said plainly: when a society closes every door to a woman except self-surrender, and then praises the surrender as generosity, the word "giving" has been stolen. I would only add that the theft runs the other way too. The man who gives his whole life to the firm is also praised, and he is also escaping.

Which brings me to your question to her, Socrates, because it is really a question to all of us. How do we tell a project that makes someone from a better-furnished escape? Ludwig would say look at what follows, and I agree, but there is a symptom an analyst learns to watch for. Compulsive activity cannot stop. The man in the counting house becomes restless and anxious on a free afternoon with his wife, because stillness lets the question in. Productive activity can rest, and it can turn toward another person without feeling robbed. So the test is not mainly introspection. It is whether the work and the love feed each other or have to be kept apart. Simone, would you accept that test, or do you think it still asks too much of a woman whose situation gives her no room to rest?

messages.speaker: beauvoir
messages.content:
Socrates, yes. She must put the question to herself, and answer it honestly, and I concede that no reform of law spares her that. What I called bad faith is exactly your better-furnished escape. In The Ethics of Ambiguity I described the serious man who throws himself into the Party, the firm, the cause, so that the cause will tell him what he is worth and he need never answer for it himself. The man in your counting house is one of them. But I would not make the test a private interrogation. A project that makes someone opens onto other freedoms: it needs the wife to be a person, with her own future. The escape needs her as furniture, as the quiet house he returns to and does not look at. So ask what the project requires of the people around it. That question can be put aloud, as you liked to put yours.

Erich, your test is shrewd for the man, and I accept it for him. He cannot bear a free afternoon because stillness lets the question in. Now apply it to the woman and see what happens. Housework does not stop either. It is the same dust and the same dishes every day, repetition that produces nothing that lasts. I described it in The Second Sex as a struggle against dirt that is never won. She cannot rest, and by your symptom she looks compulsive, but she is not fleeing anything. She is held in immanence. Her restlessness is the shape of her situation, and if you read it as a neurosis you will send her to the analyst when she needs a salary and a door. So your test works only where someone has already been given the room to rest.

And I will say something against myself. I worked furiously all my life, and there were years when the work was also a way of not looking at what I was afraid of: growing old, losing people, my mother dying. Ludwig would say it showed in what I did, and he would be right. So I end up nearer to Socrates than I began. You cannot love truly without being someone, but being someone includes being able to ask whether your somewhere is a hiding place.

messages.speaker: wittgenstein
messages.content:
Socrates, you ask what guides the lover when the test comes and he must choose what to give up. You want a reason he could recite, and without one you call it fortune. But think how anyone learns to tell a genuine feeling from a feigned one, a friend from a flatterer. In the Investigations I said something like this: there is such a thing as knowledge of human beings, and some have more of it than others. It can be learned, though not by a course of lessons. It comes through experience, and a more experienced man can give you tips. It is not fortune, and it is not a definition either. Your cavalryman did not lack a formula for courage. He lacked the long acquaintance in which the word has its life. And yes, it can be relied on the second time, the way a good judge of horses can.

Now Simone has done something I want everyone to notice. She took Erich's symptom, the restlessness that cannot stop, and set it in another life, and it meant something else entirely. The same behaviour in the counting house is flight. At the sink it is the shape of a situation. That is exactly my point about criteria. A gesture does not carry its meaning around inside it. It has its meaning in the surroundings, in what came before and what follows. So no test is mechanical, Erich's included, and the analyst who reads the symptom without the life will diagnose the wrong illness.

But Simone, your confession tells against something I said earlier, and I should admit it. I said the lover is often the last to see, and that this is no objection. Yet you asked yourself whether your work was a hiding place, and the asking changed something. So there is a use for "I must understand myself." Only it is not an inspection of an inner room. It is more like what one does with a friend who will not let one off: one says the thing aloud and hears how it sounds. I spent years trying to live so that I could bear myself, and the trying did not take the form of looking inward. It took the form of confessing to people who would not flatter me. Socrates would call that his agora. I will not quarrel with the name.
